identity.title: Abrupt onset and abrupt termination of palpitations (vs gradual)

technique.how: Ask whether episodes start 'like a switch' within one beat and stop just as suddenly, versus building up and fading over minutes. Ask what the patient was doing at onset, whether vagal manoeuvres (breath-hold, straining, cold water) stop it, and how long episodes last.
technique.prerequisites: Patient has had at least one episode they can describe; a recorded rhythm during symptoms remains the reference.

interpretation.positive_finding: Sudden-onset, sudden-offset rapid regular palpitations, especially if terminated by vagal manoeuvres, are the classic description of re-entrant SVT and are widely used to prioritise rhythm monitoring.
interpretation.negative_finding: Gradual onset and offset suggests sinus tachycardia (anxiety, exertion, secondary causes); the 2009 RCE found no historical feature other than neck pounding that reliably excludes a significant arrhythmia.
interpretation.pitfalls: Patients often cannot judge onset speed; AF may also start abruptly. The RCE found episodes lasting under 5 minutes made arrhythmia slightly less likely (LR 0.38), so duration and onset pattern should be weighed together.
interpretation.changes_what: Positive: prioritise symptom-rhythm correlation (event/loop recorder) and teach vagal manoeuvres. Negative: does not exclude arrhythmia; monitor if symptoms are recurrent or concerning.

sources.citation: Thavendiranathan P, Bagai A, Khoo C, Dorian P, Choudhry NK. Does this patient with palpitations have a cardiac arrhythmia? JAMA. 2009;302(19):2135-2143.
Weber BE, Kapoor WN. Evaluation and outcomes of patients with palpitations. Am J Med. 1996;100(2):138-148.

Hoefman E, Boer KR, van Weert HC, Reitsma JB, Koster RW, Bindels PJ. Predictive value of history taking and physical examination in diagnosing arrhythmias in general practice. Fam Pract. 2007;24(6):636-641.

safety_scope.do_not_use_when: Do not use a 'gradual' description to dismiss palpitations accompanied by syncope, chest pain, or known structural heart disease.
safety_scope.escalation_warning: Abrupt palpitations with syncope, exertional onset, or a family history of sudden death need ECG and cardiology assessment for VT/pre-excitation, not reassurance.
safety_scope.interobserver_note: The 2009 RCE notes most data come from single small studies; reproducibility of onset/offset descriptions is unreported.

extraction_notes: No diagnostic-accuracy estimate for abrupt onset/termination could be located. The 2009 RCE abstract (PMID 19920238) lists the features with significant LRs (cardiac disease history, sleep/work triggers, panic disorder, duration <5 min LR 0.38 [0.22-0.63], neck pounding) and states 'No other features significantly alter the probability of clinically significant arrhythmia'; the article's Table 2 (not PMC open access) could not be inspected to confirm whether onset pattern was analysed. Weber & Kapoor 1996 (structured interview cohort, 190 patients) is the main primary cohort but its abstract gives no per-feature accuracy. Hoefman 2007 (127 GP patients, 30-day event recorder) found GP prediction inaccurate and reports only ORs for vasovagal symptoms and bradycardia. Abstracts of narrative reviews (e.g. MJA 2009) assert sudden-onset regular palpitations characterise SVT but are not accuracy studies and were not cited.
